title: Clone N-ary Tree
statement:
You get `root`, the root of a tree in which a node may have any number of children. Every node has an integer `val` and an array `children` holding its child nodes from left to right. Return a deep copy of the tree: one brand-new node for each original node, with the same `val` and with the copies of its children in the same order. The copy must not reuse any node (or `children` array) of the original, and the original tree must be left unchanged. An empty tree (`root` is `null`) copies to `null`.

Create nodes with the provided class: `new Node(val)` starts with an empty `children` array, and `new Node(val, children)` sets it at once. The class is also available as `_Node`, the name the TypeScript starter uses for the type (that type does not list `children`; the objects still have it).

Each case is written as `[root]`, the tree serialized breadth first: the root's value and a `null`, then, for every node in breadth-first order, its children's values followed by one `null` that closes the group (a leaf contributes only the `null`), with trailing `null`s left out; an empty tree is `[]`. Your function receives the root node object, and the returned copy is shown in the same serialization, so a correct answer reproduces the input.

Follow-up: would your approach also copy a general graph, where a node can be reached along more than one path?
constraints: The depth of the tree is at most 1000
notes:
## Intuition

A tree is made of smaller trees: the copy of a node is a new node with the same value whose children are the copies of the original children. That is exactly a recursive definition, so a depth-first function that copies a node and then calls itself on each child builds the whole copy. Because every node of a tree is reached along exactly one path, no node is ever copied twice and no bookkeeping map is needed. (An iterative breadth-first copy with a queue of original/copy pairs works just as well.)

## Approach

1. If `root` is `null`, the copy of an empty tree is `null`.
2. Make `copy`, a new `Node` with `root.val` and an empty `children` array.
3. For each `child` of `root`, in order, recursively clone it and push the result onto `copy.children`.
4. Return `copy`.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree is 1 with children 3, 2, 4, and 3 has children 5, 6.

- `cloneTree(1)` makes copy 1 and loops over 3, 2, 4.
- `cloneTree(3)` makes copy 3, then copies 5 and 6 (leaves: their loops do nothing) and pushes them, giving 3 → [5, 6].
- `cloneTree(2)` and `cloneTree(4)` return leaf copies.
- Copy 1 now has children [3, 2, 4], so the result serializes to `[1, null, 3, 2, 4, null, 5, 6]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each node is copied once and each child link is followed once.
- Space: O(h) for the recursion, where h is the depth (up to 1000), plus O(n) for the copy itself.

## Pitfalls

- Returning `root`, or copying only the top node and reusing `root.children`, is a shallow copy: the copy would still contain original nodes.
- Keep the children in their original order; push them in the same order the loop visits them.
- Handle `null` before reading `root.val`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | the original node being copied in this call |
| `copy` | the new node that mirrors `root` |
| `child` | one original child of `root` |

narration.2: An empty tree has nothing to copy.
narration.3: So its copy is null as well.
narration.5: Make a new node with the same value; it starts with no children.
narration.6: Visit the original children from left to right.
narration.7: Copy each child's whole subtree recursively and attach it in the same position.
narration.9: The new node now mirrors the original subtree; hand it back to the caller.
